I plan on starting my first garden next spring, if I can find a place in the country to buy, if not will do some small gardening in my current place. What are some things you wish you knew starting out and what do you recommend for a first timer? I don't have a lot of free time, I work hard labor 60+ hours a week, and don't wish to use pesticides or herbicides.

Corn, as in maize, is brain dead easy to grow and benefits from green beans being planted with them. Water it if the temperature gets above 85 and make sure you have 5' of soil before you hit clay or bedrock or whatever. Do not grow it in a container, they will grow a stalk and leaves and will look just like the stuff in the ground, but will never grow silks so you will never get corn.

Potato towers are cool as hell but not at all cost effective and completely unnecessary. Just grow them in a pile of loose hay\grass clippings.

Start your vermiculture now, let it run all winter and this will give you a leg up on the compost that you haven't been collecting for a year or more.

Hops gets 12' high and it gets there VERY quickly. Don't try to plan to build as it grows, just have it all in place from the get go.

Pumpkins are assholes and will trample the rest of your garden. The vines grow very fast and the leaves are huge. Keep them to their own corner of the garden.

Tomatoes are best when picked from your own soil, so memorize what this motherfucker looks like right now and exterminate on sight. If you're not allergic then consider a ground bee hotel. Ground bees don't have large colonies so they can't swarm. You won't get honey, but this is about pollination and pest control so you still win.
Where I'm at now its not suitable to start a compost heap, nor would I want to move it when I buy a house next year. How should I compensate for not having vermiculture at beginning?

If you have a place to plant things outside, there are already worms. You don't have to go all out, just toss some easily composted material into the dirt and cover it. Use; vegetable scraps, banana peels, coffee grounds, tea bags etc. This will feed the worms and critters and break down into food for your plants.

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=UaajjQ0FhM4

Stackable vermiculture. Sheep manure and mulch heavily with hay, pea straw etc that breaks down quickly. You can even work it into the soil to speed things along. Be careful with buying bags of compost. I've had batches in the past that for whatever reason had waaaaay too much nutrient and fucked up the beds for a while.

use lots of much to minimize weeds. spend 5min reading about each crop you want to grow. invest in a grow light so you can start things early inside... try to plant "indeterminate' varieties of everything. try to develop a strategy up front for rotation for shorter season spring/fall crops. look into predator species which will eat whatever garden pests are in your area and order some. Build some strong trellises. you can grow a lot of vine crops vertically and maximize space. Set up a rain collection system.
Since you have a busy schedule, invest some time at the front end setting up a simple drip irrigation system that runs on a timer.

For beginner morale and limited time, you can include plenty of crops that don't take a lot of attention. Corn, beans, and garlic seem to largely grow themselves.

Success starts from the ground up, literally. Make sure your soil is the right consistency or root crops will have all kind of trouble (I learned this the the hard way).

Make lots of compost and get some rabbits. Look up Charles dowding on youtube. There are ways to do things on an extremely tight budget if you need to. What worked exceptionally well for us is a modified hugelkulture / no dig / raised bed system.

First thing we did was build a huge multi bay composting area. Our low cost solution was fencing pickets for the corners and wattle fence style walls lined with cardboard. Cover compost with horticultural plastic. We're fortunate enough to have access to unlimited decaying wood. This made the bulk of the compost. Any browns will do. Leaf mulch/litter even pine needles can be used. No shortage of weeds around for "greens". Throw in the rabbit shit/piss/hay (we use a wire cage setup with slanted roofing iron underneath and collect everything in a large container). If you're close enough to the coast check your local regs and collect seaweed to add to the compost or brew "tea" in a 44. Add a sprinkle of rock minerals occasionally when filling the bays. Of course you can add kitchen scraps, wood ash/charcoal etc.Keep an eye out for cheap or free manure. Add it in as well. If you do it right it can be ready in as little as 6 weeks. This will save you a fortune and a lot of time. This will give you soil with no deficiencies, plenty of carbon and structure and nutrients.

We had no choice but to go raised beds because of drainage issues, what we did is dug a shallow trench for each bed, filled with wood, half rotten wood and soil half way up the bed. Then layered soil, fully rotten wood and compost. Mulched heavily. If you have heavy clay soil add a bit of gypsum. We were able to instantly plant in the beds and everything grew better than anything else I've ever tried. First harvest of leafy greens 6 weeks after that. Soil drains well but holds the right amount of moisture, watering is a once a week job most of the year. Continue making compost and add a layer the beginning of every growing season.

Horticultural fleece also was a great addition that allowed us to significantly extend our growing season.

For some plants we use the gutter grow system. Fill fabric pots with the same soil/compost mix. Its much better for plants that require more space or have special needs. So tomatoes, peppers, pumpkins, melons, etc. Saves us wasting bed space.

Check out what other gardeners in your area are growing. Keep seed from your best plants as they adapt to your specific microclimate.

Start tomatoes early using heat pads and lights (a well lit windowsill will work OK as well).

We do the vast majority of germination in punnets etc. It allows you to plant the best seedlings and allow them to grow advanced enough that they just take off once in the ground. We homeschool so have a shitload of scrap paper lying around. Cut them lengthways in half and roll them into a tube ( inch and a half diameter jar works best). Fold in a bottom and lip to make a pot. We use cheap kitty litter trays to hold them. Entire pot can go straight in the ground with minimal shock to the seedlings.

As others have mentioned, look at companion planting. Like corn and climbing beans. When doing corn plant them in valleys. Once the plants are getting bigger fill in or even "hill" up around the plant with compost. The first few nodes will grow more roots and the plant will do far better having the ability to draw more moisture and nutrients.

If you're going to get into honey bees look into peaceful beekeeping using horizontal instead of vertical hives.

If you're going to do chickens either have a movable tractor or a sectioned enclosure so you can seed areas with green manure/forage.

Thank you so much for all that info. Couple quick questions, why cover the compost in plastic? Doesn't the pile need air flow? And you add weeds to your compost? Doesn't that make them more of a problem?

Plastic is to keep rain off mostly. You don't want it to get too wet. Worms etc don't like light either and probably helps with temp fluctuations.

Forgot to mention, we also made up a few PVC pipes for each bay, use a 1 in. hole saw to put holes the entire length and all around the pipe. Stand them up vertically in the bays before filling, equidistant. It definitely helps speed the process by allowing better airflow.

Our wattle/cardboard setup worked well as the air gap around the beds would have probably let them breathe. I've seen other setups using shipping pallets and shadecloth for the walls which would probably be better.

As long as the brown/green mix and moisture content is right, weeds and seeds shouldn't be a problem. The temps and biological process should take care of it all. If after the first compost you make it's still a problem, you may need to age it longer and turn the compost a few more times. There are some plants that can be a problem still, the stuff you have to burn like camphor laurel will probably survive a compost bin. Just don't put stuff like that in.

You occasionally still get a few random runners/ shoots or seeds make it through, but then you mulch heavily. I think I only had to pull out 2 weeds total in the last growing season and they were probably from the soil added to the beds not the compost.
